title: Grade 2 Maths Word Problems: The Underline-and-Solve Method + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 2 Maths Word Problems: Easy Method + Quiz
meta_desc: Solve Grade 2 maths word problems the easy way: underline, spot clue words, estimate, solve and check. Worked rupee examples plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Most Grade 2 children can add and subtract fine on paper, then freeze the moment the sum hides inside a story. Here is the exact five-step method I use to unfreeze them, with worked rupee examples and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 2 child the sum 254 + 138 and most will solve it without blinking. Now wrap the same numbers in a story — ‘Anaya had ₹254 and her grandmother gave her ₹138 more; how much does she have now?’ — and a good number of them freeze. The maths did not get harder. The reading did. That gap is exactly what grade 2 maths word problems are meant to close, and it is the single most useful thing you can practise at this age.

The reason children stall is not weak arithmetic. It is that a word problem asks them to do two jobs at once: figure out what to calculate, and only then actually calculate it. Teach those as two separate steps and the freezing stops. Here is the exact method I use, the same five steps every time, until the child runs it without being told.

The five-step method for grade 2 maths word problems

Write these five steps on a card and keep it next to the child for the first two weeks. The order matters, and step four — estimate — is the one everybody skips and the one that catches the most mistakes.

  • Underline the question. Find the actual sentence that asks something and underline it. ‘How much does she have now?’ is the target. Everything else is just information.
  • Circle the clue words. ‘More’, ‘altogether’ and ‘in all’ usually mean add. ‘Left’, ‘fewer’ and ‘how many more’ usually mean subtract. ‘Each’ and ‘every’ hint at multiplication.
  • Estimate first. Round the numbers and guess. ₹254 and ₹138 are roughly ₹250 and ₹140, so the answer should be near ₹390. Now the child has a target to check against.
  • Solve it. Write the number sentence — 254 + 138 = 392 — and work it out with the column method or mental strategy the child already knows.
  • Check it makes sense. Is 392 close to the estimate of 390? Yes. Does an answer of ‘more money’ make sense when Grandma gave money? Yes. Only now is the child done.

Clue words are a guide, not a rule

Here is the caveat nobody tells you: clue words are helpful right up until they lie. Take ‘Rohan has 120 marbles, which is 45 more than Anaya. How many does Anaya have?’ The word ‘more’ is sitting right there, yet the answer is 120 − 45 = 75. You subtract.

So I teach clue words as a first guess, never as a law. The real check is always step five: does the answer make sense? If Rohan has more, Anaya must have fewer, so the answer has to be smaller than 120. A child who reasons that way will never be fooled by a tricky ‘more’. That habit — sense-checking over keyword-hunting — is the whole game.

Worked examples with real numbers

One-step addition

‘A kirana shop sold 326 biscuit packets on Monday and 247 on Tuesday. How many in all?’ Question underlined: how many in all. Clue word: ‘in all’, so add. Estimate: 330 + 250, about 580. Solve: 326 + 247 = 573. Check: 573 is near 580, so it holds.

One-step subtraction

‘A library had 480 books and lent out 155. How many are left?’ Clue word: ‘left’, so subtract. Estimate: 480 − 150, about 330. Solve: 480 − 155 = 325. Check: close to 330, and fewer books after lending makes sense.

Simple multiplication

‘A cricket team drinks 5 water bottles each match. How many bottles for 6 matches?’ Clue word: ‘each’, and equal groups, so multiply. 5 × 6 = 30 bottles. At Grade 2 this is still repeated addition — 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 — so let the child add if the times-tables are not solid yet.

Two-step problem

This is where Grade 2 stretches. ‘Anaya bought a pencil box for ₹145 and a set of sketch pens for ₹238. She paid with a ₹500 note. How much change did she get?’ Step one: add the two prices, 145 + 238 = 383. Step two: subtract from 500, 500 − 383 = 117. The answer is ₹117. Two questions hiding inside one story — find the total, then find the change. Underlining the final question keeps the child aimed at ‘change’ and stops them stopping at 383.

A quick comparison of the clue words

Clue wordsUsual operationExample phrase
more, altogether, in all, totalAdd‘326 and 247 in all’
left, fewer, how many more, remainSubtract‘480 books, 155 lent’
each, every, groups ofMultiply (repeated add)‘5 bottles each match’
total then change, spent and leftTwo steps‘total price, then change’

How to practise without tears

In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, the fastest progress comes from fewer problems done properly, not a page of twenty rushed. Do three or four a day and insist on all five steps out loud. Let the child hold a real ₹100 note or count coins for the money problems — making it concrete does more than any explanation. And when they get one wrong, do not give the answer; ask ‘does that make sense?’ and watch them catch their own slip. That self-correction is worth ten right answers.

One more honest trade-off: two-step problems will feel too hard for the first week, and that is fine. Keep the numbers small while the method is new — a child can practise ‘total then change’ with 20 and 15 just as well as with 245 and 138. Grow the numbers once the two-step habit is solid.

Below is a free eight-question quiz built on exactly these problem types — one-step addition and subtraction, a bit of multiplication, and a couple of two-step money problems. Let your child work each one using the five steps, then read the explanations together for any they miss. quiz.intro: Eight story problems covering addition, subtraction, simple multiplication and two-step money questions. Use the five steps, then press Check my score.

questions.q: A kirana shop sold 326 packets on Monday and 247 on Tuesday. How many in all?
questions.explanation: The clue words 'in all' mean add: 326 + 247 = 573. Estimate 330 + 250 is about 580, so 573 fits.

questions.q: A library had 480 books and lent out 155. How many are left?
A cricket team uses 5 bottles each match. How many bottles for 6 matches?
questions.explanation: The clue word 'each' means equal groups: 5 × 6 = 30, the same as adding 5 six times.

questions.q: Anaya had ₹254 and her grandmother gave her ₹138 more. How much now?
questions.explanation: The clue word 'more' means add: 254 + 138 = 392 rupees.

questions.q: Rohan has 120 marbles, which is 45 more than Anaya. How many does Anaya have?
questions.explanation: The word 'more' is a trap here. Anaya has fewer, so subtract: 120 − 45 = 75.

questions.q: A pencil box costs ₹145 and sketch pens cost ₹238. What is the total?
You buy items worth ₹383 and pay with a ₹500 note. What change do you get?
questions.explanation: Change means subtract the total from what you paid: 500 − 383 = 117 rupees.

questions.q: First estimate: 298 + 203 is closest to which round number?
questions.explanation: Round to 300 + 200 = 500. Estimating first gives you a target to check the exact answer against.

faq.q: Why does my child solve sums easily but freeze on word problems?
faq.a: Because a word problem asks two jobs at once: work out what to calculate, then calculate it. Split those into separate steps — underline the question first, decide the operation, and only then do the arithmetic — and the freezing usually stops.

faq.q: Are clue words like 'more' and 'left' always reliable?
faq.a: No, and it is worth being honest about that. 'Rohan has 45 more than Anaya' contains 'more' but needs subtraction. Treat clue words as a first guess, then confirm with the real test: does the answer make sense?

faq.q: How big should the numbers be in Grade 2?
faq.a: Comfortably within 100 to 999 for addition and subtraction, and small equal groups for multiplication since times-tables are still forming. Keep numbers small when a new problem type is introduced, then grow them.

faq.q: How many word problems a day is enough?
faq.a: Three or four done properly, with all five steps said out loud, beats a rushed page of twenty. At this age the method matters far more than the volume.
